hints: Subtracting the largest available digit is always optimal; compare the optimal answers for consecutive integers.
The same long decimal blocks repeat when only the maximum digit of the fixed prefix matters.
Memoize how many greedy steps cross a block and the small amount by which the final step overshoots it.
analogy: Treat each block of consecutive numbers as a shortcut: remember its cost and where the last jump lands.
example: For 27, the largest-digit rule gives 27 -> 20 -> 18 -> 10 -> 9 -> 0, requiring 5 steps.
algorithm: Run the largest-digit greedy rule, accelerated by decimal blocks. For a block [H*10^L,(H+1)*10^L-1], memoize the number of steps and exit value when starting r below its upper end, keyed by L, the maximum digit of H, and r (0 through 8). Split a block into its ten consecutive length-(L-1) blocks and process them from high to low, carrying the overshoot into the next block; a length-zero block is one greedy subtraction. For the initial partial block, descend into the block containing n and then process the lower full blocks. Stop at zero.
correctness: The optimal step count is nondecreasing. Compare the first digit d of an optimal move from x+1 with x: if d is present in x, subtract it; if it is the newly increased units digit, x has a nonzero digit at least d-1; if a carry produced it, x ends in 9. In each case induction compares the resulting states. Consequently, subtracting the largest digit reaches a state no harder than any other choice. Each block exactly simulates this greedy process; since a step subtracts at most 9, its exit overshoot needs only nine possible states.
complexity: For D decimal digits, O(10^3 D) time and O(10^2 D) space for the memoized block states, apart from constant-size initial traversal.
